LOCAL AND GENERAL.
The Princess Royal passed a good night and her progress continues, cables Reuter under date May.4.
A meeting of the Board of Education will be held in the Board Room at the Education Office, to-morrow, at 3 p.m.

Property at Sung Wong Toi, Hill, comprising six newly-built four-storeyed Chinese houses and having an area of 5,580 sq. ft. was sold in his Auction Rooms yesterday by Mr. L. E. S. Hodge. Bidding started at $24,000 and was moderately brisk throughout. The price finally rose to $38,000, and at this figure the property was sold to Mr. Chan Tak-took.

A tragedy. occurred at Shanghai last week at the Navy Y.M.C.A. in the death of Curtis S. Foote, who was drowned in the Association pool. It appears that the young man had finished a swim and went to the shower-bath. A boy, in the meanwhile thinking that no one remained, shut off the lights. What happened in the darkened room is difficult to state. When his friends missed the deceased they returned to the pool and turned on the lights again. Mr. Foote's body was found in four and a half feet of water. First aid methods of resuscitation were applied and a Thint pulse was noticed, but it was too late and he died a few minutes later. Curiously enough a large bruise was seen on deceased's cheek and temple. How it came there is unexplained. Whether lie fell in the darkened room but the slippery tiles and slipped into the water is not known. Deceased was 24 years old, an American citizen and a native of Lawrence, Massachusetts. While in Shanghai he was connected for a time with the International Correspondence Schools.

The Coming of the World-Teacher will be the subject of this week's Public Lecture of the Hong-kong Lodge The Theosophical Society, 16, Queen's Road Central on Wednesday May 6, at 5:45 p.m. The Public are invited.

If the present line weather will continue it will be ideal for Bonnie Scotland in the Champions to-morrow and for the Dog Show on the Shanghai Band on May 16. Entries for the latter are coming in at a most encouraging rate and there is not the slightest doubt that, though it may be highly critical, Shanghai really does upsetting a dog show. A popular innovation should be the public voting for the dog considered by visitors to be the best, which will show how near the judges come to the general idea, for they will decide independently on the Champion dog.

Mr. W. J. Bonnar leaves for Home on the Hector to-day on a six months' holiday.
A first-rate story comes from Japan. According to the "Japan Chronicle," the "Asahi" reports that last year a boy of eight in Chibukken put a persimmon seed up his nose for fun. It remained there and was forgotten, but, now that spring is here, it is sprouting. Green leaves sticking out of a boy's nose were so unusual that his parents took him to the village doctor who extracted the plant. The growth of a plant in the human body is regarded as very marvellous, the "Asahi" says. It consulted Dr. Tatsumi, an authority on diseases of the throat, nose, etc. at the Osaka Medical University, who stated that he had never heard of such a thing before.

The plans for the statue of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen have been drawn up. The statue will be cast in bronze and will be six ft. six in. high and 13 in. wide. It will stand on a stone pedestal eight ft. 10 in. high, and on this will be carved the life and history of the deceased (Antonese leaders as well as his ideals and will.
The Government Veterinary Surgeon and Mrs. W. J. E. Mackenzie, left for Home by the Macedonia on Saturday.
The Committee and members of the Chinese Recreation Club are to be At Home on Saturday next at 3.30 p.m. There will be a tennis exhibition match and dancing from 6.30 to 8.30 p.m.

Many London girls were hardly more than a shuttlecock between office and bedroom, declared Mrs. Stanley Baldwin, in an appeal for a Y.W.C.A. Girls' Club to cost about £200,000, which was broadcast from 250.
Mr. Kent Clark, for a number of years the manager of the Oriental Hotel at Kobe, left for the United States on the Franconia, and it is uncertain whether he will return.
Passengers who left to-day by the Hector included Mr. C. J. Lafrentz, Mr. and Mrs. Herridge, Miss. D. Ranger, and Lt.-Cdr. Thursfield, R.N.
Mr. F. Syme $ ^{1} $ Thomson of Messrs. Dodwell & Co., Ltd., and Mrs. Syme Thomson and family left by the Macedonia on Saturday.
SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.

They were laughing at the House of Commons over the accident that happened in the member's cloueroom the other day—a tin of liquid eggs, brought in by Mr. Tom Johnston to reinforce his arguments against the importation of certain goods, had got upset in a member's new bowler hat! The incident reminds one of that in which H. G. Wells was found by a certain actor poaching an egg in his "topper" over a gas stove. "H. G." though not so gay as he once could be, can still find a smile when this is recalled.

The British Legation Chapel at Peking was crowded to utmost capacity at the memorial service to Lady Aglen last week. Bishops Scott and Norris, assisted by the Rev. J. T. Holmar, the Legation Chaplain, formerly of St. John's Cathedral, Hongkong, conducted a simple but impressive service. The entire customs staff was present as well as all the diplomatic body. Many prominent persons of a community which bears Lady Aglen in affectionate remembrance were present, and the whole assemblage was moved by deep emotion. Bishop Norris spoke a few words of appropriate gravity and the short service followed. It can be truly said that no member of the British community has done more in good works than Lady Aglen, and long will her spirit of kindness and loving care to all those in distress be remembered.

The Chinese General Chamber of Commerce has telegraphed to Peking demanding the return of the money it expended in connection with the repatriation of the troops of Chang Yuan-ming, the Ex-Defence Commissioner of Shanghai in January last.
One case of cerebrospinal fever was notified for the 24 hours ended Sunday last.

At Shanghai, Messrs. Jardina Matheson and Co., Ltd., have announced the adoption, during the summer months, commencing from the 1st inst. of the following business hours: Mondays to Fridays: 8.30 a.m. to 12. noon; 2 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. Saturdays: 8:30 a.m. to 12.noon.
His Excellency the Governor will inspect the Hongkong Police Force at 4.30 p.m. on Monday, May 18.

An armchair, similar in appearances to: "The Empty Chair," and formerly in the office of "Household Words," was among articles intimately associated with Charles Dickens, sold by Messrs. Hodgson. A writing table, from Gud's Hill Place was also sold, photographs of the articles being inscribed: "Mrs. Hulkes, with best love from Georgina Hogarth," and "Mrs. Hulkes, with Namie Dickens' best love." The articles sold for £110. A letter from Dickens to Mrs. Hulkes sending her the remainder of the proof's of the "Fade of Two Cities," with a first issue copy of the first edition, was sold for £28. "Not half a dozen of my oldest and most trusty literary friends have seen it," wrote the novelist. "It is a real pleasure to me to entrust you with the catastrophe, and to ask you to keep a grim and inflexible silence on the subject until it is published."
Mr. P. D. Wilson of the P.W.D. left on Home leave on Saturday by the Macedonia.
Lieut.-Colonel Orpen Sanders, R.A., and Mrs. Sanders left for Home on Saturday on the P. & O. Macedonia.
Jewish people like much hotter baths than Gentiles, said an attendant at Betts Street (Stepney) council baths at an inquest on a woman found dead from heart failure in one of the baths.
The forthcoming wedding is announced of Mr. Thomas McCormack, engineer, of the s.s. Ming, Sang, to Miss Charlotte Agnes Porterfield, en route from Scotland by the s.s. Sarpedon.

"When a deal man applied for a public house licence at Conville, Leicestershire, a solicitor said applicant would not likely supply two points when asked for one. 'The licence was granted to the man's wife."

The Freemasons of Bangkok entertained to dinner, prior to his departure from Bangkok on leave, Wor. Bro. J. Burns Kerr, one of the founders of the first body established there, Lodge St. John, 1072, S. C.

A message from Zarin (Nigeria) says the Prince of Wales arrived at Zaria on April 17. As a reward for his spell of piloting the train, the Prince has been presented with a mileage sheet showing ten-pence due to him, which he smilingly accepted after signing the sheet.

Raquel Meffer, the famous Spanish singer, was received in private audience by the Pope, and sang her famous song, "Pendant la Procession". (During the Procession), for which she was recently threatened with ex-communication. The Pope and the cardinals heard the song, and his Holiness gave the singer his benediction and permission to continue to sing it. The song deals with the story of a young girl who watches a religious procession and utters blasphemies, but afterwards, owing to the action of a priest, becomes an ardent convert.

Kobe's oldest foreign resident, Mrs. E. Nankivell, who had lived in the port 50 years, died last week of heart disease following an illness of six weeks. Although 78 years old, Mrs. Nankivell was unusually active for her years and up until her last illness was able to visit her many friends, few of whom knew of her advanced years. Her husband died many years ago but three daughters, two of whom were in Kobe during her illness, survive her. They are Mrs. C. H. Lightfoot of Shidzuoka and Mrs. George Grimble of Hongkong who went to Kobe when she became ill and Mrs. H. W. Millward, whose home is in London.
Miss Batten, of Bournemouth, has been licensed to drive a motor charabanc.
Fritz Baedecker, aged 81, head of the firm of Karl Baedecker, publishers of travellers' guide books, died at Leipzig on the 10th April.
West Drayton's new Baptist Church was erected at cost price by a builder, whose son drew the plans, and whose workmen accepted reduced wages.

A petition from 80,000 children enrolled by the International Goodwill Society from the province of British Columbia, urging world peace and the settlement of disputes by arbitration, has been forwarded to the League of Nations:

At the business meeting of the dramatic department of the American Women's Club, Shanghai, the following officers were elected: Mrs. S. C. Kingsbury, chairman; N. R. I. Clapp, vice-chairman and property manager; Mrs. H. V. Bernard, treasurer; Mrs. J. Scott Emons, secretary.

Two Lancashire women were discussing a visit to their town of Galli-Curci. Said one: "They do tell me as 'ow she 'ad nearly a thousand pounds for singing that one afternoon." Answered the other: "Aye, but you 'ave to remember that she's not in regular work."

A well-known Tientsin resident, (says the "P. & T. Times"), Mr. F. H. Pickwick, together with an Australian friend, Mr. Andrews, has been fishing in New Zealand. Really fishing. His bag includes a shark which tipped the balance at 224 lb., and a monster swordfish. Mr. Pickwick and Mr. Andrews hooked swordfish almost simultaneously.

A master mariner's certificate is not a thing that one usually associates with a woman, but at least one woman is a qualified "skipper." She is Lady Margaret MacRae, sister of Lord Bute, and wife of a Highland chieftain, Lady Margaret qualified some years ago, and is a well-known figure in the yachting world. She navigates her own yacht at the Cowes Regatta each year, and is an extremely competent seaman—or should it be sea—woman?

(6) That any of the said 60,000 new shares which shall not be taken up by the Company's shareholders in manner aforesaid and the remaining 80,000 unissued new shares may be issued and disposed of in such manner at such time or times and upon such terms as to ranking for dividend and otherwise as the Company's Directors shall in their absolute discretion think fit.
